content: A pathogen, also referred to as an infectious agent, is a biological entity capable of causing disease or illness in its host. This term is most commonly applied to agents that disrupt the normal physiological processes of multicellular organisms, such as animals and plants. However, pathogens are also capable of infecting unicellular organisms across all biological kingdoms. The word pathogen originates from the Greek term παθογένεια, which translates to that which produces suffering. Pathogens can invade a host through various substrates and pathways. These pathways differ in their episodic timeframes, with soil contamination being the most persistent and long-lasting reservoir for pathogens. The human body possesses numerous natural defenses against common pathogens, such as Pneumocystis, through the immune system and the presence of beneficial bacteria within the normal flora. However, if the immune system or these good bacteria are compromised—due to factors like chemotherapy, HIV infection, or the use of antibiotics targeting other pathogens—pathogenic bacteria that were previously controlled can proliferate and harm the host. Such infections are classified as opportunistic infections. Certain pathogens, such as the bacterium Yersinia pestis (associated with the Black Plague) and viruses like Variola (smallpox) and Plasmodium (malaria), have historically caused widespread mortality and significant impacts on affected populations. In modern times, pathogens such as HIV, which has infected millions globally, as well as the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) virus and the Influenza virus, continue to pose significant public health challenges. Despite advancements in medical science, including the development of vaccines, antibiotics, and antifungal agents, pathogens remain a persistent threat to human health. Social improvements, such as enhanced food safety, hygiene practices, and water treatment systems, have mitigated the risks posed by some pathogens. Types of Pathogens Pathogens can be categorized based on their structural characteristics, and each type has distinct effects on the hosts they infect. Transmission of Pathogens One of the primary mechanisms by which food or water becomes contaminated is through the release of untreated sewage into drinking water supplies or onto cropland. Individuals consuming contaminated food or water sources subsequently become infected. In developing countries, as of 2007, most sewage is discharged directly into the environment or onto agricultural land. Even in developed nations, occasional system failures can result in sanitary sewer overflows. This mode of transmission is particularly common for infectious agents responsible for diseases such as: Cholera Hepatitis A Poliomyelitis (Polio) Rotavirus infections Transmission to Vascular Plants In terrestrial vascular plants, pathogenic infections can occur through contact with foliage or via root uptake of soil-borne pathogens. The latter mechanism explains why certain plant families, such as orchids, exhibit greater resistance to disease. Orchids rely on fungal hyphae for nutrient acquisition rather than traditional root structures, which have larger radii and are more susceptible to conveying certain pathogens.
